KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 12:50 AM EST...989 mb sfc low continues 
to pull away to the N/NE of our region at this time. With our 
region still under the upper-level low (ULL) with moist cyclonic
flow aloft, latest radar imagery shows few lingering light 
showers and patchy mist/drizzle for some of the high terrain 
areas, especially near our CWA border with BTV. With widespread 
cloud cover, temperatures are in the 30s to mid 40s, and are 
only expected to drop a couple more degrees between now and 
sunrise. Skies should remain cloudy into this morning, but if 
any breaks in the clouds do form then patchy fog could quickly 
develop. 

Today, we may see a brief reprieve from the showers/mist in the 
morning as the ULL begins to slide north and east of our region, but 
another upper shortwave and area of upper diffluence approaching 
from the west this afternoon will help to reinvigorate shower 
activity. Greatest coverage of showers will be across northern 
areas, especially in the westerly favored upslope areas of the 
ADKs and southern Greens. Precipitation will be mainly rain, 
although a few wet snowflakes could mix in over the highest 
peaks of the ADKs and southern Greens. Minimal, if any, snow 
accumulation is expected for these areas. With plenty of clouds 
around, temperatures today don't look to rise too much, with 
highs in the upper 30s (terrain) to upper 40s (valleys). 

Showers come to an end tonight as heights rise aloft and a weak
ridge of high pressure builds into the region from the south. This
will lead to mainly dry conditions Sunday, and temperatures 
should be a little warmer (40s to low 50s) under transient upper
ridging. While there will be fewer low and mid clouds around 
Sunday, high clouds will be increasing, especially during the 
afternoon, ahead of our next weather system.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Sunday, a northern stream trough tracking 
through southern Canada will phase with a southern stream 
shortwave tracking across the center of the country. As these 
two features phase and become negatively tilted over the Ohio 
Valley, an associated sfc low will track through the eastern
Great Lakes and into upstate NY. Ahead of this system, strong 
low-level warm advection/isentropic lift will overlap with 
increasing moisture transport into our area. We will see areas 
of showers overspread the region Sunday evening or Sunday night,
coming to an end Monday during the day Monday. This system will
be fairly progressive. So, even with pretty impressive 
dynamical forcing, qpf amounts don't look all that high. Latest 
NBM has nudged up qpf amounts closer to deterministic guidance, 
with a widespread quarter to half inch for most areas and up to 
three quarters of an inch for some of the higher terrain areas.
Temperatures will be warm enough that precip should fall almost
entirely as rain, although as cooler air wraps into the backside
of this system we could see a brief changeover to wet snow 
across the high terrain areas of the ADKs and southern Greens. 
This would be especially true if we see some westerly upslope 
flow leading to precip lingering a little longer in these areas 
compared to the rest of the region. Regardless, only minimal 
additional snow accumulations expected in the highest 
elevations. A few additional light lake effect rain/snow 
showers can't be ruled out Monday after the main sfc low
departs, but an overall lack of moisture and relatively low 
inversion heights should prevent much in the way of lake effect 
precip reaching into our area.

The bigger story will be the gusty winds behind this system's cold 
front Monday. As the system pulls away into Maritime Canada, it will 
deepen beneath a coupled upper jet right entrance/left exit 
region. The strengthening sfc low combined with high pressure 
building in from the west will result in a tightening pressure 
gradient across eastern NY and western New England. With cold 
advection helping to support BL mixing, winds could gust in 
excess of 30-40 mph. Will continue to monitor if some wind 
advisories may be needed. The most likely locations would be for
portions of the Mohawk Valley, Capital District, and Berkshires
due to W/NW flow channeling. For these areas, the NBM has a 
30-60% chance of hitting wind advisory criteria.  Highs Monday 
should occur in the morning, with temperatures dropping through 
the afternoon in the wake of the cold front. 

Beyond this system, tranquil weather is then expected through 
at least the middle to end of next week. High pressure and 
quasi-zonal flow aloft will lead to dry conditions with 
temperatures trending back above normal for the end of the week.
The next chance for precip (rain) comes towards the very end of
the workweek or next weekend.
